messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Juan, a 22-year-old HVAC technician from a close-knit Latin American family, had always been a diligent worker, taking pride in his ability to solve problems and help others. His days were filled with the hum of air conditioning units and the warmth of his coworkers’ camaraderie. But that sense of security shattered one fateful afternoon. During a routine service call, he was distracted by a conversation with a customer and, in a moment that felt almost surreal, he failed to notice a safety hazard. The result was catastrophic: the equipment malfunctioned, leading to a serious injury for the customer. Though he had always been cautious, he had never imagined that a simple mistake could lead to such devastating consequences.

In the months that followed, Juan found himself grappling with the memories of that day. He replayed the events over and over, scrutinizing every detail as if he could uncover some hidden truth that might absolve him of guilt. Each time he tried to make sense of it, he was left feeling more detached from the reality of what happened. The memory felt alien, as if it belonged to a stranger rather than to him. He often caught himself staring blankly into space, overwhelmed by the intrusive thoughts that forced their way into his mind at the most unexpected moments. The smell of burnt metal still haunted him, triggering visceral reactions that sent him spiraling back to that day. 

Juan began to avoid anything that could remind him of the accident. He no longer attended gatherings with his friends, convinced that any conversation about work would lead back to the incident. Anniversaries associated with that day became days of solitude, filled with self-imposed isolation. He would deliberately stay away from places where he had once felt safe, preferring to confine himself to the small apartment he shared with his dog. The outside world felt dangerous, and he had come to believe that the silence of his empty home was the only thing keeping him from falling apart.

As time wore on, Juan's perception of himself began to shift. He felt unrecognizable, a shadow of the confident technician he once was. His body, which had always been a source of strength, now betrayed him with sudden surges of panic at the slightest hint of stress. A loud noise, the whir of machinery, or even an unexpected silence would send his heart racing and his palms sweating. The idea of being in a crowded place filled him with dread; he was certain that something terrible would happen if he let his guard down.

His relationships began to suffer, too. Friends reached out, but Juan’s responses grew shorter and more infrequent. He felt the weight of inaction guilt, believing he was unworthy of their concern. He would often tell himself that he should have done more during the incident, that if he had just been more attentive, the injury could have been prevented. Those thoughts echoed relentlessly in his mind, leaving him feeling trapped in a cycle of self-recrimination.

It was only after a particularly difficult week, during which he had experienced several panic attacks, that Juan began to consider seeking help. The final straw came when he found himself unable to complete a simple repair job at work. His boss had noticed his anxiety and asked if he was okay. The embarrassment he felt was profound; he realized he could no longer pretend that everything was fine. What frightened Juan most was the fear that he might never reclaim his old self, that he might remain trapped in this distorted reality forever. As he sat in the therapist's office for the first time, he held onto a flicker of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could find a way back to the person he once was.
